rule: Marathon prediction = Riegel T2 = T1 x (D2/D1)^1.06 from threshold pace treated as ~1-hour race pace, + 10 min until the athlete has a marathon result.
summary: In 2,303 recreational runners Riegel was well calibrated up to the half but at least 10 min too fast for half of marathoners, which is what the +10 min penalty corrects. Large-data work shows the fatigue exponent is individual (a fixed 1.06 is a population average) and recreational marathoners race at ~85% of critical speed (93% at 2:30, 79% at 6:00); by my own interpolation a 7:00/mi threshold (if ~CS) predicts ~3:16 on Riegel alone (~93.5% of threshold speed) and ~3:26 with the penalty (~89%), the latter closer to the ~89% the CS cohort implies for that finish time. The 'threshold = 1-hour race pace' step adds its own error; it is a feasibility estimate, not a pacing target.

sources.note: Riegel fine to half marathon; underestimates marathon time by >= 10 min for half of runners (basis for the penalty)
1.4M performances: the power-law exponent is runner-specific; individual models beat Riegel
>25k recreational marathoners raced at 84.8 +/- 13.6% of critical speed; faster runners closer to CS
Small sample (15 runners, 60 races): Riegel ~80% accuracy vs 90% for a model trained on the runner's own log
